At that price, I assumed steak would be included, so I was disappointed that it was not offered.

The meat selections included lamb, prime rib, and chicken. They were perfectly acceptable, but I felt these are foods you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money. The seafood station was more interesting, with Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at many local buffets, but I had not encountered rock crab claws elsewhere.

Unfortunately, the buffet did not provide crab-claw crackers. When I asked, staff said wooden mallets were available instead. Our table was positioned very close to another table, and I did not want to use a mallet and send pieces of crab shell toward nearby diners. As a result, I ate only the crab legs and skipped the claws.

The Asian station did not seem especially distinctive; it was comparable to the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert included gelato and assorted pastries, but nothing stood out. Fresh juices were also available, although I did not try them.

Overall, the buffet was acceptable, but I considered it overpriced for what was offered. If you are curious, it may be worth trying once—especially when there is no wait. However, if you arrive and see a long queue, I would reconsider unless the menu has changed or you particularly want to experience it.

I’ve been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life—well, the under-21 version of it—so I’ve sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

First, the good: the circular stage is genuinely smart. You’re basically looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view. That’s rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too—the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not in a “rip-off” way exactly, just... if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable feats done with maybe more clarity.

And clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don’t know. There’s a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it’s trying to say. Also, there’s way too much happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many “wow” moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing—more must be better—so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal—$99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

I agree with Misti Y-- that some people may love the Cirque shows and still dislike *Le Rêve*, although that comparison is really a separate discussion. For me, the theater and visual design are the strongest parts. The scenery and décor are breathtaking from beginning to end, and the whole concept behind the show is beautiful and appealing. Unfortunately, it doesn’t translate very well to the live performance. The storyline isn’t especially entertaining, and when I attended one performance, the stage malfunctioned repeatedly throughout the evening. That made it hard to stay engaged, even during the more impressive scenes. *Le Rêve* seems to be reaching for some of the flair and spectacle associated with Cirque, but it never quite gets there. I’d consider it mainly for the chance to experience that beautiful theater. Otherwise, you might be better off spending your money on another show.

Quick take on *Awakening* at Wynn Las Vegas: it’s fine, but not the Vegas must-see I’d build a trip around.

Aluminum conducts heat better than cast iron, meaning heat moves through it faster. That is why a thin aluminum pan heats up quickly and responds fast when you raise or lower the burner. But staying hot is not just about conductivity. It also depends on how much heat the pan can store.

A cast-iron pan is usually much thicker and heavier than a thin aluminum pan. Because it has more mass, it can hold a larger amount of heat energy. Once it is hot, adding cold food does not cool it down as quickly. The thin aluminum pan may transfer heat efficiently, but it has less stored heat to give.

For example, if you sear a cold steak, a hot cast-iron skillet often keeps sizzling after the steak hits the surface. A thin aluminum pan may lose temperature quickly, so the steak can steam or gray before browning well.

One limitation of the comparison is that pan design matters. A thick aluminum pan, especially one with a heavy base, can hold heat much better than a very thin one. So the difference is not only the metal, but also the pan’s thickness, weight, and construction.

Aluminum is great at moving heat, but that’s not the same as holding a lot of heat.

Think of heat like money. Aluminum is a fast spender: it takes heat from the burner and passes it along quickly to the food. Cast iron is more like a thick savings account. It takes longer to heat up because there’s so much heavy metal to warm, but once it’s hot, it has stored a lot of energy. So when you drop in a cold steak, a handful of mushrooms, or a wet batch of zucchini, the cast-iron pan’s temperature doesn’t crash as fast.

That’s why a cast-iron skillet can give you better browning on a steak. The meat pulls heat from the pan immediately, and the pan has enough thermal mass to keep searing instead of cooling down and steaming the surface. A thin aluminum pan may heat quickly, but it can lose temperature quickly too, especially if the food is cold or crowded.

At 3:12 every Thursday morning, Mara found the book on the flour bin.

It was always the same one: The Atlas of Vanished Islands, wrapped in a blue library jacket, its due-date card stamped so often the ink had become a bruise. She would set it by the till before dawn, and by noon someone from the library would come collect it with a sigh and a clipboard.

Tonight, while the first trays of cardamom buns breathed in the oven, Mara lifted the cover and found a note tucked at page 47.

Please don’t send it back yet. I think the island on this page is where my mother said she was born. She died last winter. I don’t know who else to ask.

Mara stood very still, dusted white to the elbows, while the mixer thumped behind her like a second heart. Outside, rain polished the empty street. Page 47 showed a crescent of land no bigger than a thumbnail, gone beneath the sea in 1891.

At five, she took a warm bun from the rack, slid the note beneath it, and placed both in the bakery window.

At 2:17 every Thursday morning, Mara found the library book on the bakery’s back step.

Always the same one: A Field Guide to North American Moths, county library sticker ghost-pale on the spine, a little flour worked into the jacket as if the book had been helping. She’d returned it twice. The librarians smiled too politely. By the third week, she kept it beside the rye starter and said nothing.

Tonight, rain ticked against the alley door. The ovens breathed. Mara was shaping croissants, palms pressing butter into dough, when the latch gave its tiny, guilty click.

No one there. Just the book, dry as a bone on the wet concrete.

She wiped her hands on her apron and opened it. A slip of paper lay between “Luna Moth” and “Promethea,” folded once.

Your window is the only light on this street. I read here until the first bus. I’m sorry about the crumbs.

Mara looked at the alley, at the dented milk crates and the steam rising off the drains. The city felt enormous for a second, then not.

She tore a corner from an order pad and wrote, Cinnamon rolls come out at 4:05.

Then she set the note inside the book, placed it on the warm windowsill, and unlocked the back door.

At 3:12 every Thursday morning, Mara found the book in the bread rack.

It was always the same one: The Practical Guide to Inland Birds, cracked blue spine, library stamp from a town forty miles away. She would set it on the flour bin, wipe butter from the cover, and mean to take it back after her shift. By noon, the errands and heat and sleep would swallow the thought.

Then, next Thursday, there it would be again, tucked between cooling rye loaves.

Tonight the bakery hummed with the proofing cabinet and the old radio’s static. Rain pressed silver lines down the front window. Mara lifted the book with both hands, as if it might be warm.

A folded receipt marked the chapter on herons.

She opened it.

In block letters, someone had written: I THINK YOU ARE THE ONLY PERSON AWAKE WHEN I AM. PAGE 47.

Mara turned to page 47. A grey heron stood in a marsh, one foot raised, patient as a saint. Under the picture, in pencil: THURSDAY, 3:30?

The clock over the mixer clicked once.

Mara brushed flour from her apron, unlocked the front door, and turned on the little OPEN sign.

A cast-iron skillet is thick and heavy, often 4 to 5 pounds, while a thin aluminum pan might weigh under a pound. Even though aluminum itself holds more heat per pound than iron, the cast-iron pan has far more mass, so it stores much more total heat.

Conductivity mostly affects how quickly and evenly heat spreads. Aluminum heats up fast and responds quickly when you turn the burner down, which also means it loses heat quickly once food hits it.

Here's a kitchen example: you preheat both pans to the same temperature and lay in two cold steaks. The thin aluminum pan's temperature drops sharply because it has little stored heat to give up, and the steaks may start to steam instead of sear. The cast-iron pan dips less, recovers faster, and keeps browning.

One limitation: this comparison isn't perfectly fair if the pans differ in size, thickness, or burner contact. A thick aluminum pan could store plenty of heat too, and cast iron can develop hot spots because it spreads heat less evenly.

Here's the thing people get tangled up on: conducting heat and holding heat are two different jobs. Aluminum is a fantastic conductor, so heat zips through it fast. But it's also light, and a light pan simply doesn't have much stuff in it to store energy. Cast iron is a mediocre conductor, yet it's heavy, and all that mass acts like a battery. Aluminum excels at this, so a thin aluminum pan heats fast and spreads heat evenly. Staying hot, however, depends on how much heat the pan has stored, and that depends mostly on mass. A typical cast-iron skillet weighs five or six pounds, while a thin aluminum pan might weigh one. Even though aluminum stores more heat per pound than iron, the heavy skillet holds far more heat in total.

The comparison has a limitation. It really pits a heavy pan against a light one rather than iron against aluminum. A thick aluminum pan of similar weight would hold comparable heat and spread it more evenly, while cast iron tends to develop hot spots over the burner.

For remote work, they need to know the right times to cut in, set up a call, and to explain a problem that they might not even fully understand yet. It's a skill (and a tough one!) to have before you have a chance to learn it.

The jrs I mentored typically improved faster if they had in person pairing, whiteboard sessions, etc. and had easy access to seniors.

I'm not trying to push for offices or anti-flexibility. Remote work can be great for self-driven devs. But for jrs, proximity is a booster that gives confidence, context, and instincts. The Vogel-Fulcher-Tammann law accurately describes critical slowing in bulk polymer glasses, but it lacks an agreed microscopic theory. We derive it from quantum mechanical transition rates, using the logarithm of final-state phase space as the activation entropy. Closed polymer chains are counted as self-avoiding polygons, while open chains anchored to surfaces are treated separately. For uniform connectivity and Flory-type scaling, the resulting activation entropy has the required energy singularity, giving the VFT form. Surface proximity lowers the dynamical singularity temperature, so films only a few nanometers thick no longer strictly obey the empirical bulk law.
